Content

What is this course about?

Modern AI systems can achieve impressive predictive performance, yet accuracy alone is not enough for trustworthy deployment. This course studies how to build and evaluate machine learning systems that are understandable, robust, and reliable, especially when models are used in high-stakes settings or face data that differ from their training distributions.

The course is research-oriented and organized around four technical themes: explainable machine learning, mechanistic interpretability, out-of-distribution generalization, and other emerging topics in trustworthy machine learning. Lectures are complemented by paper reading, student presentations, and a final research project.

Course organization

  • Section 0 — Introduction (1 week)
  • Section 1 — Explainable Machine Learning (2 weeks)
  • Section 2 — Mechanistic Interpretability (3 weeks)
  • Section 3 — Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Generalization (4 weeks)
  • Section 4 — Other Trustworthy ML Topics (2 weeks)
  • Project Presentations (2 class meetings)

Coursework

Weekly readings

  • Two core readings per week are required and provide foundational or representative coverage of the topic.
  • Further readings are optional and highlight recent advances, applications, or related work.

Student presentations

  • Each technical section will have approximately 10 recent papers or technical blogs available for student presentations.
  • Each student presents twice during the semester.
  • Presentation topics should emphasize recent and emerging trustworthy-ML research.

Presentation assignments and internal materials will be distributed through Slack.

Final project

The research-oriented course project is developed throughout the semester, with a proposal, a midterm progress presentation, a final presentation, and a written report. More than ten candidate directions are planned. To accommodate approximately 18 students in a 2.5-hour class, each midterm and final presentation will be limited to 5 minutes, followed by 2 minutes of questions and feedback. Additional project requirements and evaluation criteria will be announced during the semester.

Grading

This is a graded course. The detailed grading breakdown will be announced after the reading, presentation, and final-project requirements are finalized.
